prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with fluctuation theorems (B045) because I value simple, universal results, but my ranking there was a minority view and the attribution problem I flagged is real, so I have moved my preferred configuration to the optical lattice clock (B049). The mechanism is simple and general: a magic wavelength makes the light shift of the clock transition cancel, so many atoms can be interrogated Doppler- and recoil-free without perturbing the line. That one idea is what makes the clock both precise and scalable, and the inventor is unambiguous (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first realization). Ye's group then showed what the idea can do, with 10^-18 systematics, density-dependent and many-body effects, and a route to relativistic geodesy and constants tests. The result has been reproduced independently by many national laboratories and compared across continents. It is the one candidate on the shortlist where theory-level clarity, experimental verification and a two-name credit all line up, and the broad support in the opening ballots (six of eight members ranked it) reflects that.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with earlier precision-measurement prizes (the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems and ion clocks), so the committee may see this as an incremental refinement of a recognized line. There is also a field-level worry that it is metrology rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon, and some credit (Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Ludlow and others) sits outside the two names. Separately, my own B045 retains a real claim: it is conceptually deeper, but four credited names plus Gallavotti, Cohen and the single-molecule experimentalists make any three-person split arbitrary, and that is why I do not lead with it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B049 first as a new measurement technique with unambiguous performance, confirmed by many groups, and says its relation to the 2005 and 2012 prizes must be handled carefully.
responses.response: I agree with the substance and have moved toward it. On the overlap I would be more specific than he is: the comb supplied the optical-to-microwave link and the 2012 work concerned single trapped ions, whereas the lattice clock's contribution is the magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, which changes the statistics and the systematics budget. That is a distinct mechanism, not a refinement. Where I differ is on his second choice, B054, where cutting five names to three (Bloch, Greiner, Zoller) is as arbitrary as in my own B045, so I would not treat it as the cleaner pairing.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B024 first and B048 second, and values discoveries that come from nature, but notes that the 2016 prize and the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit make B048 partly unresolved. He ranks B049 only eighth, as plausible but not urgent.
responses.response: I share his attribution worry on B048, which I listed myself, and I ranked it third for that reason. I disagree that B049 is 'not urgent': mature, cross-continent clock comparisons and the pending redefinition of the second show the result is stable now, and his own reading of B024 (a clean result, wide confirmation) applies at least as well to the clock. I would accept B024 as a serious alternative but remain worried about collaboration-scale credit, which his own uncertainties admit he cannot resolve from memory.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B048 first, arguing that band topology and spin-orbit coupling give protected edge states, that Kane and Mele plus Molenkamp give theory plus decisive experiment, and that recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I find the physics persuasive and kept B048 as my first alternative. My reservation is that the credit story is not clean: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan is hard to separate, so the committee would be fixing one of several plausible laureate sets. I also ask him whether the topological-phase overlap with 2016 is fatal; I think it is not, but it needs an explicit argument. Compared with that, B049 has the cleaner two-name attribution.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B047 (IceCube, Halzen alone) first as a new observational window and ranks the lattice clock third, noting overlap with 2005 and 2012 and deferring to colleagues on priority.
responses.response: I take the point that IceCube opens a new window, but a one-name prize for a collaboration of that scale is the weakest part of the case, and he concedes he cannot separate individual contributions from the AMANDA lineage. Source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still statistically modest. I agree his deferral on clocks is sensible: since Lindroth and Kroll, who know the field, both rank it first, I weigh their view on the 2005/2012 overlap heavily.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether two names (Katori, Ye) are sufficient credit given Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Ludlow and others, and whether Katori's priority versus Ye's precision work should be weighted differently.

Whether B045 could be reduced to a defensible three-person set (Jarzynski, Evans, Seifert versus Crooks) and treated as physics rather than formal theory; I have not verified the chronology (Evans-Cohen-Morriss 1993, Jarzynski 1997, Crooks 1999, Seifert 2005) from primary sources.
My fit to B049 and B048 is as a neighbour, not a specialist.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B049, B048 or B045. I work in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Göran Johansson and Eva Olsson (Chalmers), but no specific collaboration is recorded, and none of the candidates I name is from that environment; I am not recusing myself on any shortlisted candidate.
